title: Review: Espolon Tequila Extra Anejo
summary:
For years, Espolon has been the tequila you reach for when you want something to use to make a huge batch of margaritas: Good enough, not expensive, 100% agave, something you can hold your head high that shelled out for an ever-so-slightly premium spirit for cocktails by the pool. The post Review: Espolon Tequila Extra Anejo appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
For years, Espolon has been the tequila you reach for when you want something to use to make a huge batch of margaritas: Good enough, not expensive, 100% agave, something you can hold your head high that shelled out for an ever-so-slightly premium spirit for cocktails by the pool.

Lately, Espolon has been pushing the brand upmarket, with both a marigold-infused offering and a $99 six-year old extra anejo called Anejo X. Now, perhaps even more confusingly than using an X to represent VI, Espolon is back with another Extra Anejo, this one aged three years but also clad in a matte black bottle. The aging is particularly unique: Two and a half years in American Oak, finished for six months in French Chardonnay casks.

Wait, this is Espolon, right? Well, let’s see what this other extra anejo expression tastes like.

Espolon Tequila Extra Anejo Review

Right away, this does not strike as an extra anejo. Tough on the nose, it is aggressively peppery and quite green. If it weren’t for the fairly dark color, you might expect this to be a young reposado expression of a punchy, Lowlands tequila. Time in glass only amplifies those notes, showcasing green pepper and, especially, green bean. After just a few minutes, any semblance of sweetness has vanished from the nose.

The palate doesn’t diverge much, if at all. After a quick burst of citrus, woody, root vegetable notes wholly dominate, an initially earthy, almost muddy quality building quickly to a crescendo. It’s all quite one-note, though ashy creosote soon creeps in, only amplifying the vegetal nature of the spirit. Any sense of fruit or sweetness is, again, quite fleeting and soon forgotten, the finish almost acrid with bitterness, raw vegetation, and freshly cut grass.

80 proof. NOM 1440.

C+ / $70

title: Review: Copper and Cask X Bourbon 10 Years Old and Batch 17 Cigar Blend Bourbon
summary:
Great whiskey depends on more than grain, water, time, and wood. Just as important is the judgment and expertise of the person who brings those elements together. It is an often-overlooked part of whiskey-making, yet it can be the difference between a collection of good barrels and a finished whiskey that stands apart. Copper &…

The post Review: Copper and Cask X Bourbon 10 Years Old and Batch 17 Cigar Blend Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Great whiskey depends on more than grain, water, time, and wood. Just as important is the judgment and expertise of the person who brings those elements together. It is an often-overlooked part of whiskey-making, yet it can be the difference between a collection of good barrels and a finished whiskey that stands apart.

Copper & Cask sources its whiskey and makes it its own through the blending expertise of Barrel Master Stephen Corrigan. His work requires an understanding of how individual barrels complement one another, which flavors deserve greater prominence, and when the various components have come together as intended. Blending is not simply a matter of combining whiskeys. It is about recognizing what each barrel brings to the table and determining how its contribution can serve the finished product.

That philosophy offers an interesting perspective on two very different Copper & Cask releases. Batch 17 of the Small Batch Series Cigar Blend Bourbon brings together four finishing casks: Armagnac, Port, Cognac, and Sherry. Batch X-01, meanwhile, is a 10-year-old bourbon with an entirely different story to tell. Each release presents Corrigan with its own set of blending decisions, providing an opportunity to examine two approaches to whiskey-making and the results they yield.

Let’s take a closer look at both 2026 releases and see what Corrigan has put together.

Copper & Cask X Bourbon 10 Years Old Review

Batch X-01 is a particularly impressive example of what can be accomplished with well-aged MGP bourbon and an experienced blender at the helm. Comprised of 45 barrels distilled in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, this release brings together two bourbon mashbills, with every barrel aged for at least 10 years and 3 months. The oldest barrels date back to July 2014, having spent 12 years and 1 month in oak.

The barrels initially matured in Kentucky and Indiana before spending their final 2 to 6 months at Copper & Cask’s facility in Providence, Rhode Island. Approximately 60% of the blend consists of bourbon distilled from a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley. The remaining 40% comes from a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley.

Before the final assembly, the barrels were blended in micro batches, some of which were allowed to marry for as long as three months. The finished blend then spent approximately one month marrying before bottling.

The nose opens with cocoa butter, bringing a mildly nutty, chocolate-like quality that brushes up against pecan pie filling. Interestingly, the nuttiness isn’t particularly identifiable as pecan or any other specific variety. Vanilla pudding skin joins the mix before the bouquet takes a rather pronounced turn toward mulled, unfiltered apple cider. The apple cider is the primary attraction here, with the fruit itself taking precedence over the accompanying mulling spices. Given some time in the glass, the cocoa butter and unfiltered apple cider become the leading aromas, working exceptionally well together. It’s an outstanding opening and one that makes spending time with the glass particularly enjoyable.

The palate starts with butterscotch and gingerbread, providing an great combination of sweetness and spice. Chocolate frosting and maraschino cherries arrive across the mid-palate, supported by a medium-thick viscosity. Cherry remains prominent through the finish, where the spice component transitions toward cherry cola, with the syrupy cherry quality taking precedence. Pear and bread-like animal cracker notes follow, before a late appearance from strawberry hard candy brings the tasting experience to a close.

From the first nosing to the final notes of the finish, Batch X-01 delivers an excellent bourbon experience. Oak, fruit, and spice are represented in pleasing proportions, and the progression from cocoa butter and apple cider to cherry cola and strawberry candy gives the whiskey plenty to offer. It’s the sort of bourbon that should appeal equally to seasoned enthusiasts and those who simply enjoy a well-made pour without spending time dissecting every component.

Perhaps the most impressive part of this release, however, is its price.

Historically, MGP bourbon was often valued at approximately $10 per year of age. That informal pricing benchmark eventually went out the window as the bourbon market became increasingly inflated, with bottles routinely commanding considerably more. Batch X-01 offers something of a refreshing departure from that trend. Here is a high-quality bourbon aged between 10 and 12 years, priced well below that traditional $10-per-year benchmark.

It’s an excellent whiskey at a very fair price, and one that tastes considerably more expensive than its retail tag suggests. For anyone looking to add a well-aged MGP bourbon to their collection without paying an inflated premium, Batch X-01 is an especially attractive purchase. 116.4 proof. A / $70

Copper & Cask Cigar Batch 17 Cigar Blend Bourbon 9 Years Old Review

Batch 17 is a blend of 33 barrels distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, with all barrels having aged for at least 9 years prior to finishing. Approximately 80% of the blend consists of bourbon distilled from a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley. The remaining 20% comes from a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley.

Before finishing, the youngest barrel had been filled in June 2017 and aged for 8 years and 4 months. The oldest was filled in October 2016 and had reached exactly 9 years of age.

The blending process began with micro batches of 4 to 6 barrels. These smaller groups were assembled prior to cask finishing, with each micro batch adhering to a single mashbill. From there, Barrel Master Stephen Corrigan selected bourbon matured in various finishing casks for inclusion in the final blend.

Oloroso Sherry and 20-year-old Armagnac account for approximately 40% each, making them the primary finishing components. Tawny Port and 25-year-old Cognac each contribute approximately 10%. The final blend was allowed to marry for roughly two months before being bottled in September 2026, although some of the smaller components had up to an additional two months of marrying time before the final assembly.

The finishing casks make their impact known immediately on the nose. Luxardo cherries jump out of the glass, accompanied by a potent muscovado sweetness. That initial concentration of sweetness gradually gives way to dark chocolate, which introduces a slightly bitter counterpoint. Arriving later, burnt orange peel adds a touch of citrus zest to the bouquet. The combination makes for an especially interesting wintertime pour, with the darker, sweeter aromas providing plenty of substance while the orange peel offers a zesty lift above the sweetness.

The palate opens with Rolos candy and dried figs. Black cherry soda takes over through the mid-palate, bringing a fruity sweetness that is kept in check by accompanying black pepper. The mouthfeel is notably dense, but the whiskey never crosses into syrupy territory.

The finish continues that progression, introducing espresso and orange zest to provide some contrast against the sweeter elements. Prunes and sweet cinnamon eventually bring the tasting experience to its conclusion, leaving the final portion of the pour with a decidedly fruit-forward profile.

Stephen Corrigan has put together an exemplary release for the cigar blend category. Among the cigar blends I’ve tasted in 2026, particularly those incorporating several varieties of finishing casks, Batch 17 is arguably the best I’ve encountered.

That praise comes with an important qualification. I generally don’t gravitate toward cigar blend bourbons featuring numerous finishing casks. Too often, I find these releases overwhelming, with excessive sweetness and a syrupy quality that distracts from the bourbon itself. As a result, cigar blends rarely rank highly when I’m evaluating the bourbon category as a whole. Even when one performs well within its own category, that doesn’t necessarily translate into the sort of whiskey I want to reach for on a regular basis.

Yet Stephen Corrigan has managed to change my opinion on more than one occasion. Between Copper & Cask and Wheel Horse, he has assembled several releases that I’ve genuinely loved. More importantly, these are bottles I enjoy as bourbon, rather than simply considering them good examples of cigar blends. That’s a meaningful distinction in my evaluation of this category.

For consumers who actively seek out cigar blend bourbons, Batch 17 is a 2026 release that should be on their shopping list. Corrigan has demonstrated considerable skill in bringing together four very different finishing casks without allowing their contributions to overwhelm the underlying bourbon. That’s no small accomplishment, and it’s precisely why this release earns such high marks from me. 118.4 proof. A- / $80

title: Review: Wines of Famiglia Casadei, 2026 Releases
summary:
Judging strictly by the documentation furnished on its website, and there’s a good deal of it, Famiglia Casadei’s commitment to authentic wines and ethical products is legitimate and uncompromising. No one has to take this on faith: the timeline and receipts are right there. The family photo at the top of the Famiglia’s website puts…

The post Review: Wines of Famiglia Casadei, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Judging strictly by the documentation furnished on its website, and there’s a good deal of it, Famiglia Casadei’s commitment to authentic wines and ethical products is legitimate and uncompromising. No one has to take this on faith: the timeline and receipts are right there. The family photo at the top of the Famiglia’s website puts people on notice that they are not playing around and that there is zero interest in entertaining the cynics. They say what they mean. Even the dog appears ready to handle the toughest biodiversity questions with ease. Along with a staunch commitment to principles, the grapes used in their wines originate from numerous regions, resulting in quite a depth of portfolio. Today we’re trying three of their latest, including an Italian GSM.

2024 Olianas Cannanou DOC – 90% Cannonau (Grenache) and 10% Tintiliu. Aromas of wild berry at first, though give it a few minutes and a cigar box squeaks open, followed by a small piece of dark chocolate. Lively acidity and soft tannins support a core of dark cherry and red plum on the palate, melded together with some baking spice. It’s easy company straight out of the bottle but give this a bit of a chill and pair it with a Manchego or Gruyère to heighten the experience. B+ / $23

2021 Castello del Trebbio Chianti Rufina Riserva DOCG – Layered and restrained, with aromas of blackberry and sour cherry followed by black pepper and herbs. Dark fruit leads the charge on the palate, supported by chalky tannins and ample acidity before being accompanied by a note of licorice rope as it recedes. Straightforward, approachable and delivers the goods. There’s very little with which to find fault. B+ / $27

2023 Tenuta Casadei Sogno Mediterraneo GSM IGT – Dense and right from the onset, this one is a beast. It needs a good hour before enjoying so it can find its footing. A big blast of balsamic at first, then tar and wild mushroom as it opens up, along with a hint of violet if you are patient enough to wait for it. But it’s the palate where it gets deep and complex: currants, ripe blackberries and a drizzle of dark chocolate. A GSM blend from Italy? Quite the anomaly, but what is even more surprising is the quality found at this price point. Shockingly good, but can use a rich dinner to reinforce its quality.  A- / $25

The post Review: Booker’s Bourbon “Milkshake Batch” 2026-02 and “Southern Thunder Batch” 2026-03 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We’re behind on new Booker’s releases, so we’re ganging up the latest pair of releases in this head-to-head look at two offerings, both landing at about the 7 1/2 year-old mark. Details on each (and an explanation of their names) follow alongside our reviews.

Booker’s Bourbon “Milkshake Batch” 2026-02 Review

Perhaps an obvious one: Booker Noe loved milkshakes, and this namesake offering hits the bottle after 7 years, 6 months, and 12 days in barrel, blended from four production runs, all warehoused separately. The name also feels apt, as there’s a certain chocolate bent to the finished product, evident on the nose alongside a more strenuous vanilla character. Racy cinnamon and nutmeg amplify the sweeter side of the whiskey, lightly smoldering barrel char lingering in the nostrils.

The chocolate element pops right away on the tongue, and though the whiskey is naturally on the boozy side, it doesn’t overwhelmingly feel hot. Water is helpful all the same, tempering any overt pushiness and letting the sweeter side to be revealed of what is increasingly a seductive and cheery bourbon. Brought down to about 100 proof or so, a dark caramel-toffee quality becomes prominent, the finish reminiscent of Skor candy bars, though further analysis sees an even sweeter conclusion — vanilla cake frosting, approaching butterscotch — emerging into view. Dialing in the right amount of water tempering takes more than a little doing.

I’d love to have seen more fruit on this whiskey; as it stands, there’s just a hint of maraschino cherry that flits in and out of view, chased off by touches of tobacco. All told, though, it’s a high-end expression in the series. 124.4 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Booker’s Bourbon “Southern Thunder Batch” 2026-03 Review

I will let you guess who “Southern Thunder” describes. This whiskey is aged 7 years, 8 months, and 14 days, pulled from a collection of five batches from four different rickhouses. Booker’s almost goes two for two with this release, which is bombastic on the nose — heavier on char and savory elements compared to 2026-02 — with a clear tobacco note that becomes increasingly smoky the longer it sits in the glass. Eventually the whiskey settles heavily into this groove, though it remains a little off-putting thanks to its even toastier bottling proof, which hits the nose heavy on the barrel.

The palate offers a bit of a twist. Savory, almost beefy to start, a latent sweetness offers notes of citrus peel and Maraska cherry, hinting at anise, later more strongly at clove. Caramel dominates as the body fills things in, with more cherry and spice filling in the gaps. Again, finding the perfect amount of water is a worthwhile endeavor, which balances out notes of nougat, spice, and fruit — but only if you work at it. At cask strength, the barrel remains overtly dominant, though it ultimately lands on notes of dried banana, with which I think every last one of us has an arm’s length relationship. 127.3 proof. B+ / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Wines of Larkmead, Autumn 2026 Releases
summary:
Larkmead sits on an unassuming stretch of Calistoga, at the end of a lane sharing its name, and has spent over a century being one of the more interesting places in Napa Valley without ever making a grand spectacle of it. This is unusual, and it’s a little suspicious: the region is thick with estates…

The post Review: Wines of Larkmead, Autumn 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Larkmead sits on an unassuming stretch of Calistoga, at the end of a lane sharing its name, and has spent over a century being one of the more interesting places in Napa Valley without ever making a grand spectacle of it. This is unusual, and it’s a little suspicious: the region is thick with estates adorned with sculpture gardens, helicopter pads, and founder’s tales that have clearly been through legal review. But unlike some, if not most, of them Larkmead has a good name and a cast of characters.

The land started as part of a thousand-acre Hitchcock family holding, and it was Lillie Hitchcock Coit (San Francisco socialite, firefighter fanatic, eventual benefactor of Coit Tower) who named the place and furnished it with nineteenth-century attitude. The Salmina family turned it into a working winery in 1895, won awards at the 1915 World’s Fair, and made it through Prohibition by making sacramental wine, a workaround suggesting either profound faith or deft understanding of federal paperwork, maybe both. The Solaris bought the property in 1948 and have not left: Kate Solari Baker and her husband Cam tend to the land, leaning heavily towards Cabernet. The Firebelle, named for Lillie, and the Solari Cabernet tell opposing tales of the same soil. Wine writers lunge at the word “storied” for moments like this, and I will concede that the word is accurate. But a place this old, still run by one family, still making wine this good, makes the adjective feel underwhelming. It needs somebody to just get down the lane and experience it all firsthand. But make a reservation first.

2023 Larkmead Solari Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley – The year’s Solari arrives with a lot on its mind. Black currants lead, running through the glass with swagger, and then the rest of the cast files in: tobacco leaf, pine needles, sage and if you’re patient enough, graphite. The tannins are abundant and also, improbably, silken: a structure most wines spend years trying to compose and this one seems to have been born with. Give it time in the glass and it opens into something more herbal, finishing dry and earthy and a bit tart. Everything here points toward the long haul, and the structure to get there is already well established. Drink it now if you absolutely must: it will keep your attention and a good portion of your evening pleasantly occupied. But the smart money rests on storing it away somewhere dark and cool and forgetting about it. Do not worry: this wine will have plenty left to say in a few year’s time, probably all the better.  A / $200

2023 Larkmead The Lark Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley – Open this Solari young and you’ll find it in a dark and rather serious mood: dense with graphite, anise and currants stacked up front, with charred oak following not too far behind. Giving it at least an hour in the glass is a must. Tart plums and blackberry step forward on the palate, followed dark cherry and milk chocolate. The tannins turn supple, and the finish lands somewhere earthy and bright, with the dark fruit continuously oscillating with the savory elements. With some aging, the oak and chocolate should recede into the background, and everything currently talking over each other will have learned to take turns. It is a fine argument for patience, and, if your bank account can take the hit, an even better one for buying two bottles: one to open now, out of curiosity, and one to leave alone, out of well-earned faith. Pour it now and enjoy the show or start planning for one incredible evening around late Autumn 2031.  A / $300

title: Review: Jose Cuervo Reserva de la Familia Private Cask Collection Tequila Edition No. 2 Mole Cask (2026)
summary:

Edition No. 1 incorporated tequila aged in Colombian oak casks, a real rarity that, frankly, I’ve never heard done before. Three years later, Cuervo is finally back to this collection, finishing anejo tequila in mole…

The post Review: Jose Cuervo Reserva de la Familia Private Cask Collection Tequila Edition No. 2 Mole Cask (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
In 2023, Jose Cuervo released a special edition of its Reserva de la Familia Tequila called the Private Cask Collection. Edition No. 1 incorporated tequila aged in Colombian oak casks, a real rarity that, frankly, I’ve never heard done before. Three years later, Cuervo is finally back to this collection, finishing anejo tequila in mole casks — barrels seasoned with mole.

Mole Cask is hand-crafted in small batches at La Rojeña, the world’s oldest tequila distillery. It begins with 100% Blue Weber agave. Each piña is hand-trimmed with the jicama cut, leaving only the sweet central core. The agave is slow-roasted in masonry brick ovens built in 1812 before it is fermented with proprietary yeast and twice distilled. The tequila ages in New American and French oak barrels, before finishing for three to four months in red Oaxaca mole-seasoned medium toast new American oak barrels. The resulting Añejo Tequila mirrors the classic mole character, drawing notes of cacao, spice, dried fruit and pepper into the spirit imparted through slow contact with virgin oak.

Ready to get your mole in my tequila? Here goes.

Jose Cuervo Reserva de la Familia Private Cask Collection Tequila Edition No. 2 Mole Cask (2026) Review

There’s something unmistakably different about this tequila, as well you should expect given the way it is made. Rich and chocolatey on the nose, there’s an instant connection with mole from the start, the tequila backed up with spices ranging from cloves to cinnamon to red pepper. Immense and immersive, it undulates with layers of red fruit and a minty quality that pairs beautifully with the chocolate notes — classic mole, really.

The palate surprises, dropping ample fruit to start and very little in the way of the classic mole flavors evident on the nose. Greener, herbal agave comes into focus soon after the fruit hits, the grassy notes touched with vanilla and caramel sauce. Toasted coconut emerges on the finish, giving the palate a much more traditional anejo character than the nose would suggest. That’s not a bad thing, as a little mole can go a long way, both in cooking and, it turns out, in tequila. A sharp bite of raspberry informs the lengthy and pleasant finish.

All told, this is one of the most unusual tequilas to hit our doorstep in recent memory. What could they possibly come up with next?

80 proof. NOM 1122.

A- / $120

summary:

Case in point: This newly released Napa cabernet. Almost archetypical in its construction, this 2023 cab bursts out of the gate with dense notes of currants and black cherries, tempered…

The post Review: 2023 John Anthony Cabernet Sauvignon Napa Valley appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
You may know John Anthony only from his low-cost brand, JaM Cellars — but Anthony also makes luxe, cellar-worthy wines that deserve more serious attention. Case in point: This newly released Napa cabernet.

Almost archetypical in its construction, this 2023 cab bursts out of the gate with dense notes of currants and black cherries, tempered with notes of cloves and black tea. A graphite-heavy quality builds from there, sliding into layers of dark chocolate and almost burnt caramel sauce. All of this could be a bit overwhelming, but the finish sees some brightness in the form of orange peel and a hint of bitter-tart grapefruit peel. Fans of classic Napa cab will find no fault here.

A- / $85

title: Review: Jefferson’s Reserve 8 Years Old
summary:
Big-ish things are happening over at Jefferson’s. The entire lineup has gotten a glow-up with bolder packaging featuring larger typeface. I never minded squinting to read my Jefferson’s labels, but I guess we bourbon drinkers are all getting older by the day. There’s also been some streamlining of offerings, with both the flagship rye and…

The post Review: Jefferson’s Reserve 8 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Big-ish things are happening over at Jefferson’s. The entire lineup has gotten a glow-up with bolder packaging featuring larger typeface. I never minded squinting to read my Jefferson’s labels, but I guess we bourbon drinkers are all getting older by the day. There’s also been some streamlining of offerings, with both the flagship rye and bourbon now falling under the Very Small Batch label. The biggest changeup, however, goes to fan favorite Jefferson’s Reserve, which now carries an 8-year age statement and a not insignificant uptick in proof.

The former Jefferson’s Reserve sported a small print subtitle “Very Old Very Small Batch,” but it was always somewhat unclear what they meant by “very old” with some sources mentioning 8- to 20-year-old bourbons in the blend. When the limited-edition Cask Strength expression of Jefferson’s Reserve arrived last year, it boasted an 8-year age statement, as well, so perhaps they are leaving the older stock out of the mix altogether now. Let’s see if we can taste any difference.

Jefferson’s Reserve 8 Years Old Review

The nose is perhaps fresher than the original with less oak and more sweet grain. That’s not to say it comes across younger. It wears its minimum eight years well, but the highlights are certainly less oak driven and more focused on the corn with top notes of warm cornbread muffins and caramel corn fresh out of the pan. Vanilla bean blooms with time in the glass and a bit of damp oak and baked apple finds its way into the bouquet eventually, but those sweet, corn notes never let up.

The palate is similarly single minded at first with an initial rush of buttery candy corn underpinned by lush notes of pecan pralines and dark caramel. It’s light but mouth-coating with a richness that builds across the sip. The grain gives way to citrus on the midpalate, but things stay candy sweet with sugared orange peel that evolves to orange creamsicle in short order. The sweetness almost overwhelms before a generous nuttiness tempers things slightly with notes of creamy peanut butter fudge and butter brickle ice cream. It’s all a bit decadent but comes together with finesse on the finish, delivering a warm fadeout of toffee, corn pudding, and honey roasted peanuts. Its impressive approachability may be the only thing that resembles the Jefferson’s Reserve of old, but I’m not complaining.

96 proof.

A- / $50 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena
summary:
Packaged in a 750ml wine bottle with a Champagne style cork, you could be forgiven for assuming MaraBela was a new sparkling wine, albeit perhaps with a new age bent. It’s not, though, it’s tea: sparkling tea, specifically, designed as a non-alcoholic alternative to a traditional bottle of bubbly. Per the brand: MaraBela wasn’t created…

The post Review: MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Packaged in a 750ml wine bottle with a Champagne style cork, you could be forgiven for assuming MaraBela was a new sparkling wine, albeit perhaps with a new age bent. It’s not, though, it’s tea: sparkling tea, specifically, designed as a non-alcoholic alternative to a traditional bottle of bubbly.

Per the brand:

MaraBela wasn’t created in response to trend data. As an athlete who regularly goes through periods without alcohol, Co-Founder Jesús Martínez Bujanda wanted something he genuinely enjoyed at the table when he wasn’t drinking. But this new research does reinforce the family’s decision to create a dry, 0.0% sparkling tea built around complexity, ritual and food.

At 12 calories per serving, it’s perhaps the most harmless beverage you can enjoy short of a glass of water. Let’s give it a try.

MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena Review

On the nose, the beverage is quite innocuous, barely there as it lingers in glass. Time helps the tea’s herbaceous qualities come to the fore, the product offering a clear mix of black tea leaf and fresh herbs, though it never approaches anything overwhelming, remaining quite mild long after it’s been poured.

The palate offers a clearer, slightly stronger character that shows off a mix of red berries — strawberry and raspberry notes predominant. In time, more floral notes begin to dominate on the tongue, along with a lemon peel quality that finally evokes the verbena in the recipe. The finish is quite bright and very refreshing: You could easily polish off a bottle of this at dinner without thinking twice. (Though my recommendation is to serve it over ice, to help keep it cold.)

A curious and fun N/A alternative to wine, it’s not quite the same as drinking a dealcoholized sparkling wine (of which there are many good options), but it’s definitely a more elegant and nuanced option than, say, a bottle of Martinelli’s.

A- / $20

content:
Blending bourbon and rye used to be a wild novelty, but now it’s surprisingly commonplace, perhaps due to the runaway success of High West’s Bourye, which has become an annually released, prized commodity among those in the know.

The latest to jump into the blending game is Bulleit, whose new Bulleit ’87 is in some ways a throwback to the Reagan years. While the brand would take years to reach prominence, it was actually launched in 1987, well before the bourbon boom was on anyone’s radar.

This is a new core expression (the first since 2011) entering the permanent lineup, blending standard Bulleit Bourbon (from Kentucky) and Bulleit 95 Rye (from Indiana) in unstated proportions. Both the bourbon and rye are aged for at least four years, “finished separately in their original barrels with toasted American oak and French oak staves for four to six weeks, then blended together and bottled in Shelbyville, Kentucky.”

Let’s dive in.

Bulleit ’87 Review

My primitive thoughts on the brand from nearly 20 years ago aside, today’s Bulleit isn’t known for being an aggressive whiskey, and ’87 is probably the softest expression in the Bulleit arsenal to date. The nose is quite buttery, with immediate shortbread overtones, though a low-level smokiness slowly comes into view with time in glass. Rye spice elements make an appearance, with a whiff of cherry pits later. Cloves linger.

The palate again kicks off as quite soft and understated, more brown butter than fresh, some popcorn, caramel, and a dusting of spice. The whiskey never really picks up from there, as fruitier elements come into the picture — baked apples, sugared pears, and just a hint of golden raisins on the back end. As is the case with the nose, the rye-driven spice doesn’t appear much at all until the finish begins to near, with cinnamon and clove notes, punctuated with the occasional plump red berry, pop into the fore. None of it really lasts, though, the finish returning to those buttery, biscuity notes, with Bulleit ’87 ultimately fading from view with the impression of a cookie. A whiskeyish cookie, but emphasis on the latter.

The bottle’s a mixer, but a solid and versatile one, to the point where it feels like that was entirely the point in its creation. The name may confuse everyone who sips it. In a cocktail — of which I’ve had a few — the idea should come across with ease.

90 proof.

B+ / $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]
